h: Names cut, streets sealed: who is taking away democracy's space?
dek: Habib Siddiqui argues that the closing of Jantar Mantar, the cutting of crores of names and the heavy police presence are all parts of one story: the shrinking of democratic space.
body: The writer begins with the picture of thousands of young people who wanted to reach Delhi to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and who were stopped on the way. According to him, Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and pushed people towards Ramlila Maidan, Burari and other distant grounds. The Supreme Court had to ask the Centre and the police for an answer.

Siddiqui says Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the Cockroach Janata Party were sent to jail for climbing a barricade and waving the Tricolour. According to the writer, more than 26 thousand paramilitary personnel and 6 thousand Delhi Police personnel were deployed, Central Park in Connaught Place was shut, and movement was stopped at eleven Metro stations. The mood reminds him of the days of the Emergency.

At the root is the SIR. It is alleged that about 13 crore (130 million) names were removed from the voter rolls in it. The writer cites Prannoy Roy's Decoder analysis: in Bengal, the seats where the most names were cut showed nearly double the swing against the ruling party, women made up 62 percent of the names cut, and Muslim names were cut at a rate 52 percent higher than others. The Commission denies any political motive.

The writer also suggests a remedy: a forensic audit by an impartial body, public rules and algorithms for weeding out names, door to door checks before names are cut on a large scale, and easy ways to restore names, especially for people on the margins.

Finally, he counts both the strength and the weakness of the movement. The message is simple, save the vote, and young people have moved past fear. But citing Erica Chenoweth's study, he reminds readers that successful nonviolent movements usually reach three and a half percent of the population, and there is still a long road ahead here.
nazar: This piece adds something important: cutting names and closing roads are not two separate decisions but one way of thinking, in which the citizen is removed first from the list and then from the public square. If women and Muslims make up so many of the names cut, this is not a technical glitch. It is a question about equal citizenship.

The Chenoweth warning is not a light one either. The movement will have to go beyond Jantar Mantar to the small towns, the bastis (poor settlements) and the homes whose names were cut, because they are the real witnesses.
sawal: How does someone whose name was cut from the list reach the public square?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission's fresh check of voter rolls. It is alleged that a large number of genuine voters lost their names in it.
The three and a half percent rule
A study by political scientist Erica Chenoweth, according to which nonviolent movements with the active participation of this share of the population have often succeeded.
ank: names reportedly cut in the SIR
higher rate at which Muslim names were cut

h: Laughter in the face of the lathi: when the young start mocking power
dek: Swarna Bhatnagar writes that amid barricades and lathis, the laughter of slogans, video games and reels has become this movement's sharpest weapon.
body: The writer is herself one of those whom the government used all its might to stop from reaching Jantar Mantar. A day or two later her sister sent her a video game called 'Chalo Jantar Mantar' (On to Jantar Mantar), in which the player has to break through a police cordon to get there. After a whole day of being pushed around on the street, breaking the same blockade on screen felt like fun to her.

Bhatnagar argues that power builds its aura with barricades, lathis (police batons), convoys of police and uniforms, so that disobedience looks frightening and costly. Laughter and satire scatter this hollow awe. She cites the Russian thinker Mikhail Bakhtin's idea of the 'carnival', those moments when laughter brings the powerful down and ordinary people mock their rulers.

The movement's language is an example. Posters were made on the NEET irregularities, and in October a rhyming slogan against Gyanesh Kumar about 'one kachori, two teas' rang out. A film dialogue became 'Gyanesh, ho gaya bhai' (Gyanesh, that's enough, brother). Games such as 'Bhaag Neha Bhaag', 'Digital Dhapli' and 'Digi Tiranga' also came out, in which a player can wave the Tricolour without fear of arrest. The writer asks why simply flying the flag in the capital has become a cause for conflict.

She accepts that a joke cannot break an iron barricade and a game cannot wipe out court cases. Still, what James C. Scott called the hidden resistance of the weak is now out in the open. Recalling Emma Goldman, she says there is no point fighting for a freedom that takes away the joy of life.

Finally, Bhatnagar calls it mental laziness to dismiss her generation as screen addicts or naive. These people were never in any party, yet they are answering the lathi with song and the baton with music. They can be put in jail, but their spirit cannot be enslaved.
nazar: What a dictatorship fears most is not protest but being laughed at, because laughter cracks the wall of fear. When power detains those who wave the Tricolour and the young turn it into a game, it becomes clear who holds the moral high ground.

But the price behind the laughter must also be remembered: court cases, bail dates, and the students from poor families and small towns who cannot afford a lawyer. The movement's good humour will last only if a structure of legal aid and solidarity stands alongside it.
sawal: Can laughter bring down the wall of fear?
ref: Carnival
An idea of the Russian thinker Mikhail Bakhtin: occasions when the laughter and fun of fairs and festivals turn the order of rank and power upside down for a while.
Hidden transcript
James C. Scott's term for the ways oppressed people resist their rulers without open conflict, through everyday jokes, songs and tricks.

h: Yes, I am guilty: of turning away from the news
dek: A personal confession from Priyanka Gupta in Serbia: staying away from politics is also taking a side, and the small inconvenience of protest is the price of democracy.
body: Priyanka Gupta was going to write a light letter about her travels. On 10 October, in the Serbian city of Niš, her phone filled up with videos of the protests in Delhi, and she had to admit she had known nothing about this whole voter roll issue. From here the piece becomes a confession.

She talks about her apolitical upbringing, about avoiding student politics at IIT Delhi, and about quiet protests that stayed limited to personal choices. Then she sets out the SIR figures: according to her, more than 13 crore (130 million) names were removed from the draft rolls of 30 states and union territories, and two of the three election commissioners recorded objections several times. In her reading, Muslims were hit hardest.

An argument in a WhatsApp group leads her to bigger questions: is permission needed for a protest, and does the inconvenience to ordinary people make a protest wrong? Her answer is that Article 19 gives the right to peaceful assembly, that permission rules cannot become a weapon to stop every protest, and that bearing a little hardship for someone else's cause is a citizen's moral duty.

Then she adds up accountability: deaths from collapsing bridges, the country's slide on indexes of women's safety and press freedom, and more than seven thousand detentions in one week. Mentioning student suicides after the NEET paper leak, she asks why the burden of stopping leaks should fall on children.

Finally, recalling Bhagat Singh, she says the first step is to stop what is wrong, and that attention should be on the movement rather than on faces. Her crime, in her words, was keeping her eyes turned away from the news.
nazar: This piece is not by an expert. It is a voice of the educated middle class that has believed until now that politics is someone else's job. The real test of this movement is whether such people break their silence or not.
Silence is not a neutral place. Those whose names were cut often have neither a voice nor a platform, so the silence of people who are safe works against them.
sawal: Is staying silent also a way of taking sides?
ref: Article 19
The part of the Constitution that gives the freedom to speak, to assemble peacefully and without arms, and to form associations, subject to reasonable restrictions.

h: Questions from the street, and the duty to answer them on the street too?
dek: A J Prabal argues that Mohan Bhagwat lectured protesters to find solutions but stayed silent on the grievances that have brought people onto the streets.
body: This Qaumi Awaz column begins with the RSS's centenary celebrations, which were completed on Dussehra on 20 October. According to the organisation's annual report, it has reached 10 crore (100 million) families in 4.61 lakh (461,000) villages and towns. But according to the writer, this year has not been easy for it, because the Gen Z protests in June and then the nationwide movement against 'vote theft' took it by surprise.

Prabal recalls that in August Bhagwat had called the young people 'our own youth', while in his Vijayadashami speech he described them as emotional, misguided and led astray by foreign influence. He called the present wave a storm from the West and hinted at a foreign hand behind it. Most surprising of all, according to the writer, Bhagwat put the responsibility for solving the problems on the protesters.

A large part of the column is about double standards. The writer asks why an organisation that calls itself the world's largest non-governmental organisation does not give details of its registration, membership, donations and audits, when thousands of NGOs have had their registration cancelled for minor reasons. It also mentions the Karnataka government's notice and the jibe by the state's minister Priyank Kharge, who asked for a proper application and permission for route marches.

According to the writer, Bhagwat's speech made no mention of the vote theft allegations, the SIR of the voter rolls, or the alleged irregularities in the CBSE and NEET exams. There was concern about rumours on social media, but silence on the role of the mainstream media. Quoting writer Ashutosh, the column recalls that in 1975 the Sangh itself supported Jayaprakash Narayan, so was that not a campaign for regime change? Journalist Dhirendra K Jha sees in this speech a fear of losing power.

The final question is simple: if citizens are asking for solutions to their problems, why is it not the government's job to answer? According to Prabal, before expecting solutions from protesters, the grievances that forced people onto the streets must be addressed. Calling the movement a foreign conspiracy or the work of misguided youth is no answer to these questions.
nazar: The 'foreign hand' charge has been thrown at every movement that asks those in power to account for themselves, from the farmers' movement to the sit-ins against the citizenship law. When the country's most powerful organisation does not say a word about the names cut from the voter rolls, that silence is also a statement.

In a democracy, the person with a grievance is not asked for a solution. They are heard. Those whose names have disappeared from the rolls are the poor, workers and minorities, and it is the Commission and the government that must answer their grievance.
sawal: How did the one asking for accountability become responsible for the solution?
ref: SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. The opposition has alleged large-scale irregularities over the names cut in it.
Vijayadashami speech
The RSS chief's speech in Nagpur every year on Dussehra, seen as setting the Sangh's direction for the year.

h: 75 years since the first election: turn doubt into proof, and let the Commission answer
dek: Piyush Pandey finds the vote theft allegations weak on evidence, but also says the questions raised over the SIR cannot be brushed aside as noise.
body: India's first general election began on 25 October 1951. Amid poverty, illiteracy and the wounds of Partition, giving every adult the vote was a revolutionary step. Piyush Pandey regrets that on this 75th anniversary, instead of celebration, there are questions over the Election Commission's fairness, and the opposition is accusing Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of helping the ruling side through the SIR.

The writer recalls that quarrels between the Commission and the government are not new. In 2009 the then Chief Election Commissioner N. Gopalaswami recommended the removal of Navin Chawla, and former commissioners such as T.N. Seshan and M.S. Gill later entered politics on Congress tickets. There was also an era of booth capturing, which EVMs largely ended. Voters grew from 17.3 crore to nearly 98 crore.

Pandey then questions the vote theft story. In his view, a narrative is being built from a few incidents without full evidence. He points out that after Gyanesh Kumar took charge, TVK won in Tamil Nadu and the Congress-led alliance won in Kerala, so an opposition victory is not impossible. He also lists the contradictions in opposition unity, such as the clash between the Congress and the Trinamool in Bengal.

The writer also has doubts about the direction of the movement. He mentions Neha Bora's reference to Bangladesh and Prashant Bhushan's words about 'regime change', and says a campaign that began with NEET turned within a few months into a demand to remove Gyanesh Kumar.

Still, his conclusion puts responsibility on both sides. The opposition should say on which seats how many genuine voters were cut and what happened to the complaints. The Commission should set up clear reasons for cutting names, hearings, easy appeals and decisions within a fixed time, because the questions raised over the SIR are not just political noise.
nazar: This piece leans against the movement, and that is why it is worth reading: it has all the arguments that supporters of the government are making. But the opposition winning a few states does not prove that the voter rolls are clean. The question is not about election results. It is about the worker, the woman or the minority voter whose name was quietly cut without them even knowing.

The burden of proof has also been turned upside down. When the Commission itself put the burden on citizens to prove their eligibility, the first duty of transparency lies with it. The conditions the writer suggests, that is reasons, hearings and easy appeals, are exactly what the people sitting on the streets are demanding.
sawal: Who should prove a name was wrongly cut, the voter or the Commission?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, a drive to check voter rolls afresh. It is alleged that a large number of genuine voters lost their names in it.
Booth capturing
Seizing a polling station by force to cast fake votes. It was a common complaint in the 1980s and 1990s, and EVMs reduced it a great deal.

h: Within the law or in its absence: which side is this protest on?
dek: Former law minister Salman Khurshid argues that this movement is not about breaking rules but about returning to them, and that its next test will be both on the street and in the Supreme Court.
body: Salman Khurshid is a senior Congress leader and a former law minister, and this column is written from that side. He starts with a legal distinction: a decision is either within authority or outside it. In his view, protest too either works within the rule of law or is a response to its absence, and this movement demanding accountability from the Chief Election Commissioner stands right on that line.

Scenes of lawyers being dragged by their hands and feet shake him. He asks whether the country has moved beyond dissent to some other turning point. He says the police seemed more interested in stopping rights than securing them, though their duty is both.

He recalls that at a special Sunday hearing on 11 October, the Supreme Court eased needless restrictions on movement, reaffirmed the right to protest and said lawyers too could join the protests. Khurshid calls this a fight not only over election law but over constitutional morality, and recalls satyagraha (Gandhi's nonviolent resistance).

He sees the rise of the Cockroach Janata Party as a special feature of this movement, but says it is too early to tell whether it can grow beyond scattered protests into a lasting challenge. In his view, this fight is not about rejecting rules but about returning to basic principles.
Finally, he sees two currents in the country: one plural and inclusive, the other seeking uniformity. The coming months will test both the street and the highest court.
nazar: Khurshid's point matters: the protesters have not come out to bring down the system but to remind it of its own rules. What the government calls anarchy is really a demand to return to the Constitution.
But his own party's record on institutions in its time was not spotless either, so this trust will be built only if the opposition holds to these same principles when it returns to power.
sawal: When an institution itself breaks the rules, where does the citizen go?
ref: Constitutional morality
Loyalty to the values of the Constitution, equality, liberty and fraternity, which courts use as a test in disputed cases.

h: Protest pushed out of town: a trick to keep dissent out of power's sight
dek: Nagendra shows how protest sites from Delhi to Lucknow and Patna have been steadily pushed to the margins, and the removal of Jantar Mantar is the latest link in this chain.
body: Nagendra begins by saying that protest is not just a crowd on the street. It is the citizen's presence before power. When an old protest site is lifted from the centre of power and sent to the edge of the city, the matter is no longer only about traffic or security. The question becomes whether the voice of the movement is being kept away from the ears of the government.

The writer lists a long history. In Lucknow, protests were once held near the Vidhan Bhavan (state assembly), then moved to Jhulelal Park and Lakshman Mela Maidan, and in 2018 to Eco Garden, far from the city. In Patna, Bailey Road's 'Hartali Mod' (strike corner) was left behind, then R-Block, then Gardanibagh, and now there are reports of plans to move it even further. In Delhi, first the Boat Club was closed, where Mahendra Singh Tikait's big farmers' sit-in was held in 1988, and now Jantar Mantar.

According to the piece, after 12 October protest sites in Delhi have shrunk to Ramlila Maidan, Burari and a ground in east Delhi. Jantar Mantar was close to Parliament and the ministries, which is why many national movements became known across the country from there. In 2018 the Supreme Court chose regulation there instead of a total ban.

Nagendra also gives the examples of Hyderabad's Dharna Chowk, Chennai's Marina, Mumbai's Azad Maidan, Bengaluru's Freedom Park and Jaipur's Statue Circle. From Mumbai he draws the lesson that a fixed place can be kept in the middle of the city while still putting conditions on numbers and timing. Pushing protests far away is not the only way.

His conclusion is that a protest site is not a piece of land but a platform for dialogue between citizen and power. If it is made so distant, inconvenient and controlled that it is hard to reach and hard to be heard there, the question is not about city management but about the place of dissent in a democracy.
nazar: On paper the right to protest survives, but in practice it is sent where neither ministers, nor the media, nor ordinary passers-by will see it. This is the cleverest form of restriction, because no ban needs to be announced.

It hits hardest those who have no TV studio or social media power behind them: farmers, contract workers, ASHA and anganwadi (village health and childcare) workers, students from villages. In a ground on the edge of the city, their voice is reduced to an echo.
sawal: If a protest cannot be seen, who will hear it?
ref: Boat Club
The ground near Rajpath that for decades was the centre of big political and farmers' movements in Delhi. Gatherings there were banned after the 1988 Tikait sit-in.
Jantar Mantar
The road beside an 18th-century observatory near Parliament, which from the 1990s was the country's best-known protest site.

h: Israel's election: the face may change, the policy will not
dek: Diana Buttu says that whether Netanyahu wins or loses in the 27 October vote, nothing will change for Palestinians, and change will come only from outside pressure.
body: Israel votes on 27 October, and the contest is being shown as one between two camps, one with Netanyahu and the other against him. Diplomats abroad assume that if Netanyahu goes, the way will open for a two-state solution and the rebuilding of Gaza. Palestinian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu calls this hope an illusion.

According to her, after three years of a war she calls genocide, and despite cases going on in the international court, these questions are not on the election agenda at all. Candidates who back Netanyahu openly talk of wiping out Gaza and making the West Bank the same, and their campaigns proudly show pictures of demolished homes and hunger.

The opposition is no different, is her second argument. She recalls that Avigdor Lieberman has talked of blocking food to Gaza and occupying Lebanon, and Yair Golan opposes international recognition of Palestine. No major candidate has a Palestinian state on their agenda. The only debate is how much the Haredi community should share in the war and how much Palestinians should be punished.

Buttu asks what kind of society elects leaders who speak openly of war crimes. Her answer is that from Israel's founding until now, there has been no price to pay for seizing land, killings and collective punishment, so all this has become normal. The world's silence has sent the message that what is happening is acceptable.

So her conclusion is that change will come not from the ballot box but from outside. She calls for wide economic and political sanctions on Israel. In her view, if the world does not give up its policy of silence and concessions, then whichever camp wins, the slogan of occupation, dispossession and building settlements will remain government policy.
nazar: The Indian government keeps deepening its deals with Israel on arms, technology and sending workers, and it is often assumed that the problem lies with just one leader. Buttu's argument reminds us that occupation is not one face's policy but a system. A country that once stood against colonialism must ask whether it stands with this system or with the people who are its victims.
sawal: If both camps have the same policy, what is the election about?
ref: Two-state solution
The proposal to create an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel, long seen as the basis of international diplomacy, but steadily weakened on the ground by the spread of settlements.
Haredi
Israel's ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities, who were long exempt from military service. There is a bitter political fight over this exemption during the war.

h: The Iran war and a retreating American empire
dek: According to Tom Engelhardt, Trump is retreating on every front, from warships leaving the Gulf to the November election.
body: Well-known American anti-war writer Tom Engelhardt begins with a strange piece of news. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted to broadcast live the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist convicted of the Fort Hood killings. After protests the broadcast plan was dropped, but not the execution. The writer recalls that the US military last carried out such a sentence in 1945, and wonders which countries the US will stand beside on the list of those that carry out executions in public.
For him, this spectacle is part of a bigger picture: an empire on the downslope on a warming planet. In sharp satire, he calls Trump a living example of imperial decline.

The biggest proof is the Iran war. Trump had promised a quick victory, but the war has gone on for seven months. The writer cites reports in American newspapers that US warships have been called back from the Gulf and bombers from a base in Britain. Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Rubio are now saying this war could drag on through Trump's whole term.

Engelhardt also mocks the argument of an Iranian nuclear threat. In his view there was no such threat, yet the war goes on in its name, and Trump talks fancifully about attacks on Los Angeles and San Diego.

The writer predicts that the Republicans will lose badly in the 3 November midterm elections, because Trump's own voters are staying home. He says that when a superpower retreats like this, the world has already changed, whether or not we can see it.
nazar: The Iran war is not distant news for India. When oil coming through Hormuz gets costlier, everything from cooking gas to fares gets costlier, and the livelihoods of lakhs of Indian workers in the Gulf are at stake. Engelhardt's satire shows that the power on which the world order was said to rest is itself stumbling. At such a time India should build its own independent path and a voice for peace instead of following any one superpower.
sawal: Who really pays the price when a superpower loses?
ref: Fort Hood killings
In 2009, army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan opened fire at the Fort Hood military base in Texas and killed 13 people. A military court sentenced him to death.
Midterm elections
Elections to Congress held in the middle of a US president's term, seen as a public verdict on the government's work.

h: Invent an enemy, collect the votes: the cost of the politics of fear
dek: Muhammad Mohsin Iqbal writes that when governments cannot defend their record, the noise of an outside threat becomes the easiest way out.
body: Muhammad Mohsin Iqbal, director general of library and research at Pakistan's National Assembly, makes a simple argument. In a democracy, elections should be fought on jobs, prices, education and healthcare. But when a government has no work to show, it invents a story of an outside enemy, in which criticism can be called treason and restraint called weakness.

He gives the example of India's 2019 election, when the Pulwama attack and the Balakot strike took over the whole campaign and the ruling party presented them as proof of strong leadership, while the opposition questioned the claims and their political use. According to the writer, when inflammatory statements take the place of investigation and diplomacy in both India and Pakistan, the room for decision-making between two nuclear-armed neighbours shrinks dangerously.

This is not only South Asia's story. The writer threads together Netanyahu's security politics in Israel, the false claims before the invasion of Iraq, Argentina's military regime that attacked the Falklands in 1982, Putin's rise in popularity after Crimea, and Turkey's cross-border operations. In Argentina, the war first brought a surge of nationalism, then defeat brought down the regime itself.

He accepts that not every crisis is manufactured, but a permanent language of emergency lets governments avoid answering for unemployment, prices and the state of institutions. India and Pakistan both face big economic and social challenges, and politics that turns hostility into an electoral need eats up the money for human development and the trust of both societies.
His conclusion is that a true statesman knows the difference between a real security need and electoral gain. Fear can bring a short-term gain, but generations pay its price.
nazar: This piece was written from across the border, but India will see its own face clearly in it, and so will Pakistan. On both sides TV studios build a war mood, and the bill is paid by people in border villages, soldiers' families, and the crores of people whose school and hospital budgets go into weapons. The next time a crisis flares up just before an election, the first question should be whose accounting it is helping to put off.
sawal: Without an enemy, what would our leaders ask for votes on?
ref: Pulwama and Balakot

In February 2019, 40 personnel were killed in a suicide attack on a CRPF convoy in Pulwama. India then carried out an air strike in Balakot in Pakistan, which became a major issue in that year's general election.
Falklands War
In 1982 Argentina's military government attacked the British-held Falkland Islands. After its defeat by Britain, military rule there ended the very next year.

h: Pakistan: a scattered PTI and a government wielding the stick
dek: A Dawn editorial says the internal chaos of Imran Khan's party makes talks impossible, but the government's harshness is making things worse.
body: In its editorial, the Pakistani newspaper Dawn puts both the country's largest opposition party, the PTI, and the government in the dock. According to the paper, since Imran Khan went to jail the party has failed to act wisely at every key moment. As long as Khan could talk to his workers, he blocked every step that would weaken his own standing. Later the government closed off that channel too, but nothing improved.

Talks between the government and the opposition broke down at the last minute, and governor's rule was then imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The government alleges that the PTI changed its demands at the eleventh hour. In recent days, a senior office-bearer resigning and then returning, and a senator leaving the party's WhatsApp groups, are examples of this disarray.

The most interesting point of the editorial is that the party's biggest weakness is also its strength. Only Imran Khan can run the PTI, so any meaningful talks with the government are possible only with him. The paper says the government refuses to accept this truth.

Dawn says clearly that trying to crush the PTI with arrests and legal tactics is wrong in principle and backfires in practice. It gives the party a chance to strengthen its claim of being a victim, and a mainstream party cannot be wiped out this way. On top of that, it eats away the democratic space on which the government itself stands.

The government also has no story of its own, such as better policies or sound management of the economy. According to the paper, ordinary citizens are trapped between a scattered opposition and a directionless government, and any hope of relief is still far off.
nazar: This picture from next door should not feel strange to us. Cases against opposition leaders, sidelining elected state governments and the stick in place of talks: this formula is being tried in many places in South Asia. Dawn's point that trying to wipe out the opposition ultimately hollows out the very democracy on which the government's own legitimacy rests is just as true for India.
sawal: How long can a democracy run with the opposition in jail?
ref: PTI
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, Imran Khan's party. Since 2023 Khan has been in jail in several cases, and the party faces constant government action.
Governor's rule
In Pakistan, removing a province's elected government and handing power to a governor appointed by the Centre, somewhat like President's Rule in India.

h: At Jamia, the fight for a students' union is a fight for the institution's soul
dek: Aman Ahmed and Aziz Umar explain why the demand for a students' union, shut for twenty years, has now reached a hunger strike.
body: On 24 October at Jamia Millia Islamia, staff and security guards entered the sit-in where a hunger strike was under way demanding the restoration of the students' union, and students formed a human chain to protect the hunger strikers. According to the writers, a week earlier guards and Delhi Police had beaten and removed several students in the early hours, five of whom had been without food for several days.

Jamia's students' union has been shut since 2006. So why this anger now, twenty years later? The writers' answer is the saffronisation of the campus. They mention the April 2026 RSS-linked Yuva Kumbh event attended by the Vice-Chancellor and the Registrar, and the 2017 iftar, after which action was taken against students who protested the invitation to RSS leader Indresh Kumar. They say meetings of other student groups were stopped again and again.

The piece recalls that Jamia grew out of the Non-Cooperation Movement, where people like Zakir Husain came back to teach without pay. According to the writers, this legacy is fading. They cite the present Vice-Chancellor's ABVP past, allegations of political links in appointments and the lack of transparency in hostel allotment, though they themselves admit that many of these allegations are not yet proven.

In 2012 a petition was filed in the Delhi High Court to hold elections, and in 2017 the demand was raised again, but for nearly two decades there has been no elected body at the university level. In the present structure the Dean is the ex officio president and holds a veto, which the writers call half a democracy.

They accept that a students' union will not solve every problem, but it will create an accountable platform where decisions can be questioned. The aim is not to replace the administration but to rebuild trust.
nazar: A students' union is democracy's first school, and its being shut for twenty years at Jamia is not just about one campus. Across the country, university elections are being put off, police are being called in on sit-ins, and appointments are being made by ideology. At a Muslim minority institution this pressure is double, because every dissent there is viewed with suspicion. The demand of these hungry students is very small: just an elected platform to have their say.
sawal: How can a campus afraid of the vote shape citizens?
ref: Jamia Millia Islamia
Founded in Aligarh in 1920 during the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements, it later moved to Delhi. It became a central university in 1988.
Indresh Kumar
A senior RSS pracharak (full-time worker) and patron of the Muslim Rashtriya Manch, a Sangh-linked body that claims to work among Muslims.

h: A glass of tea in Sudan's war, and an inherited habit of care
dek: Sudanese writer Ahmed Ismat Ahmed, living in Cairo, says war can burn homes but cannot erase the habit of caring for one another.
body: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed was a spokesperson for the resistance committees in Sudan's 2018-19 revolution and now lives in Cairo after fleeing the war. His personal essay begins at a tea stall on the edge of Cairo, where he meets his friend Mahmoud. The two embrace for a long time, and a young woman they do not know, sitting nearby, starts to cry.

To hide his embarrassment, Mahmoud starts showing a video of Khartoum burning on his phone. The writer says this is a habit of Sudanese living abroad, the body in one place and the mind in the home that is burning. From here he opens up the story of his generations: a grandfather from Wadi Halfa, drowned for the High Dam, who started a school under a tree, and a mother who did not give up her studies even after her father's death, and finished her veterinary degree while carrying the writer in her womb.

In his days at the University of Khartoum, the real politics happened not in classrooms but at the stalls of the tea women who knew how every student was doing. The writer admits he once thought you had to be hard to survive, but in fact it was care that kept people alive. During the movement, activists kept an informal ledger: who was missing, who needed medicine, who had not eaten.

He says care cannot be bought or sold, and that is why power fears it. The essay turns on one small moment: without asking, Mahmoud orders a second tea and sugar for the writer, the Khartoum way in which the other person is looked after before they have to ask.

At the end, a child straightens a crooked poster on the wall of a half-built school, without thinking, because someone once looked after him too. For the writer, this is the legacy no war can take away.
nazar: Sudan's war is the world's largest displacement crisis, yet it rarely finds space in our news. This essay reminds us that refugees are not numbers but people carrying their memories and relationships with them. In India too, people uprooted by riots, evictions and floods often stand by each other before the government does. This politics of care, which writes down the names of the hungry and the missing in a ledger, is the strongest foundation of any movement.
sawal: What do uprooted people save and carry with them?
ref: Resistance committees
People's committees formed in Sudan's neighbourhoods, which led the 2018-19 movement that brought down Omar al-Bashir's dictatorship and took on relief work during the war.
Wadi Halfa
A town in northern Sudan that was drowned in the 1960s by the lake of Egypt's Aswan High Dam. Thousands of Nubian people from there were resettled elsewhere.

h: The Adivasis' doctor is in jail: the price of opposing the Sijimali mine
dek: Dr Randall Sequeira, who has treated people in Adivasi villages in Kalahandi for years, and Dalit activist Laxman Naik were picked up at night and jailed in a case over a clash in April.
body: On the night of 16 October, Odisha Police picked up Dr Randall Sequeira and Dalit activist Laxman Naik from a rented house in Bhawanipatna. According to the report, the police came in two jeeps, many of them in plain clothes, and both men's phones were seized. Their families and lawyers did not know where they were until the next evening. Then a magistrate in Rayagada sent both to 15 days of judicial custody.

The case concerns a clash on 6-7 April in Kantamal village in Rayagada district, when police went to the village to get a road built for Vedanta's proposed Sijimali bauxite mine. Villagers allege that lathis and tear gas were used. The police say they were attacked. The two men were not named in the original FIR; the police say their role came out during the investigation. The charges include attempt to murder, rioting and even dacoity (armed robbery).

DIG Akhileshwar Singh alleged that instead of treating people, the doctor was inciting Adivasis (indigenous people) against the government. The PUCL and several civil society groups called the arrests repression and demanded their release. According to activists, more than a hundred Dalits and Adivasis have been arrested and 43 cases filed since the protests began in 2023.

Dr Sequeira has run health camps in Kalahandi since 2017 and has treated pregnant women and malnourished children. Villagers allege that the gram sabha's consent for the mine was obtained with forged signatures.
nazar: When the very presence of a doctor in an area becomes a reason for suspicion, understand that the real case there is about land. More than a hundred arrests in Sijimali show that those who speak against mining are being isolated one by one, and anyone who stands with them is also called an 'instigator'.
sawal: Since when did treating Adivasis become incitement?
ref: Sijimali block
A bauxite block spread across Rayagada and Kalahandi, which the Odisha government auctioned to Vedanta in 2023.
Gram sabha consent
In Fifth Schedule areas, a project like mining needs the consent of the village's general assembly. In the Niyamgiri case the Supreme Court treated it as decisive.

h: Rent only to Hindus: a Bhopal notice, and still no FIR
dek: It has been 48 days since a complaint about a communal notice in a Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana housing society, but the police have not registered a case.
body: At Bhopal's No. 12 bus stop, the municipal corporation has built a housing society under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (the Prime Minister's housing scheme). A notice went up there 'by order of the committee', asking house owners to prefer Hindu families when renting out. Strikingly, the land on which this society stands was acquired in 1962 from the family of 50-year-old Pyare Khan.

Pyare Khan filed a complaint at Habibganj police station on 3 September. Even by 23 October, that is 48 days later, no FIR had been registered. He went to the police station four times and was sent from one officer to another each time. One policeman said a case would be registered after an inquiry. The law says that for a cognisable offence the FIR is registered first, and if a preliminary inquiry is needed, it must be completed within 14 days.

The municipal corporation washed its hands of the notice and said maintenance is in the hands of a temporary resident welfare association. The notice came down about three weeks later, but no one apologised. The report recalls that when the accusation is against Muslims, an FIR for hurting religious sentiments is registered almost at once.
nazar: An order to choose tenants by religion in a colony built with public money, followed by a month and a half of police silence, looks like two separate laws: one for those whose sentiments get hurt, and one for those whose sentiments no one cares about. Registering an FIR is not the police's choice. It is their duty.
sawal: Whose complaint gets an FIR at once, and whose does not?
ref: Cognisable offence
An offence in which the police can arrest without a warrant and must register an FIR as soon as they receive information. The Supreme Court made this clear in the Lalita Kumari judgment.

h: No medical report, no compensation? High Court strikes down the condition
dek: The Allahabad High Court has said a rape survivor cannot be denied compensation just because she refused a medical examination.
body: In 2024 an eight-year-old girl was allegedly raped. When the case was registered, she did not consent to a medical examination. The accused has been arrested and the trial is on. But when she sought compensation under the rules of Uttar Pradesh's Rani Laxmibai Mahila Evam Bal Samman Kosh (a state fund for women and children), the state rejected her application on the ground that there was no medical report.

On 23 October, a bench of Justice Saral Srivastava and Justice Garima Prashad declared unconstitutional the very condition that made the FIR, the chargesheet and an injury report confirming sexual assault mandatory. The court said that under POCSO, visible injury is not needed to prove the offence, and the claim can be checked from the FIR and the chargesheet.

The bench cited Section 184(7) of the BNSS, which gives a survivor the right to refuse an examination. According to the court, the condition forced a survivor to choose between the right over her own body and relief, and by splitting survivors of the same crime into two classes, it violated Article 14. The state was ordered to pay three lakh rupees within ten days.
nazar: Welfare schemes often turn into a wall of paperwork, and the highest wall stands in front of those who are most broken. This ruling is a reminder that a survivor's 'no' is also her right, and relief cannot be given at the cost of that right.
sawal: Why should a survivor have to pawn her own body to get help?
ref: BNSS Section 184(7)
A provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita under which a rape survivor's medical examination can happen only with her consent or her guardian's.
Article 14
The equality article of the Constitution. Treating people in the same situation differently without a solid reason is seen as a violation of it.

h: Sahil Wakode's death: 84 groups ask IIT Bombay's director to resign
dek: An open letter alleges that within hours of his death the institute branded the Dalit student a cheat, and defended the accused professor while the inquiry was still on.
body: Sahil Wakode, a second-year B.Tech student at IIT Bombay, was found dead in his hostel on 18 September. The same day, Professor Suryanarayana Doola had accused him of cheating with a phone in an exam. His family and the protesting students allege that Sahil faced constant caste-based mental harassment. On his parents' complaint, a case has been registered under the SC/ST Act and for abetment of suicide, but a month later no one has been arrested.

Now 84 organisations and 40 individuals have written an open letter to the director, Prof. Shireesh Kedare, asking him to resign. They make four charges: within hours of the death, the institute called Sahil a cheat in a press statement; the faculty forum openly backed the accused while the inquiry was on; CCTV footage from the exam hall was selectively passed to the media; and police pushed and shoved the students protesting at the gate, along with Sahil's parents.

The signatories include groups such as the Ambedkar Students' Association, AIDSO and the Dalit Students' Union of the University of Hyderabad. Deepali Salve of AIISCA said that on 25 October the groups will gather to demand the arrest of both the professor and the director.
nazar: From Rohith Vemula to Darshan Solanki and now Sahil Wakode, each time the institution's first worry is its reputation, not the student's life. Calling someone a 'cheat' on the very day of his death is passing judgment before any inquiry. Until accountability is fixed from the top, campuses will remain places of fear for Dalit students.
sawal: Why did the institute pass judgment before the inquiry?
ref: Darshan Solanki
A Dalit student at IIT Bombay who died in February 2023. His family too had alleged caste discrimination on campus.

h: Siang dam protest: villages turned into camps, a headman sacked, accounts blocked
dek: In Arunachal, Adi farmers standing against an 11,000 megawatt dam face a tightening grip of preventive detention, paramilitary camps and social media bans.
body: The Siang Upper Multipurpose Project was proposed by NITI Aayog in 2017 as an answer to China's Yarlung Tsangpo projects. According to the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum, it will affect 27 villages, and the forum has blocked surveys for years. Anger flared after Chief Minister Pema Khandu's visit in September; vehicles were burnt and a legislator's house was vandalised.

On 9 October, four activists, including forum leader Adum Tayom, were picked up from a barber's shop in Pasighat, and an order was passed for up to six months of preventive detention under a state law. According to the report, at least 40 FIRs have been filed since 2025, and a 65-year-old protester alleges his ribs were broken in custody.

Villagers say hundreds of paramilitary personnel are deployed in Beging, Parong, Riga and Yingkiong, and identity cards are checked even on the way to the fields. Facebook accounts of journalists and activists were blocked on the Centre's orders. A gaon burah (village headman) says he was removed for not signing consent to the survey; the deputy commissioner denies this.
nazar: The first price of a dam built in the name of national security is being paid by the very people who have lived on that border for centuries. Consent taken with guns and sackings is no longer consent. The Siang question is not only about electricity; it is about who will decide on the land of the Northeast's Adivasi (indigenous) people.
sawal: If the people whose villages will drown are not asked, who is the dam for?
ref: Adi community
The main Adivasi community of Arunachal's Siang region, whose farming, settlements and faith are tied to the Siang river.
Yarlung Tsangpo
The name of the Brahmaputra in Tibet. China is building a huge dam there, and India presents a dam on the Siang as its answer.
photo_note: Representative image: a river in Arunachal

h: Seven thousand farmers in Akole: five thousand rupees of drought relief is not enough
dek: 265 of Maharashtra's 358 talukas have been declared drought-hit; the Kisan Sabha surrounded the tehsil office demanding loan waivers and crop insurance payouts.
body: On 22 October, in Akole in Ahilyanagar district, about seven thousand farmers, farm labourers and women walked to the tehsil (sub-district) office and handed over a memorandum along with thousands of applications. The march was led by the All India Kisan Sabha, CITU, AIDWA and DYFI. Their demands include compensation for crop loss, immediate insurance payouts, a waiver of up to two lakh rupees for farmers who repaid loans on time, and land titles for those who till forest land.

Brinda Karat, Ashok Dhawale and Ajit Nawale called the state's drought relief of five thousand rupees far too little, and alleged that the four thousand rupees of the Namo Kisan Nidhi have also been held back. The sit-in will continue until 26 October, and if the demands are not met, they warn of a march from Akole to Mumbai.

The state has declared 265 talukas drought-hit. Between 1 June and 25 September, rainfall was 18 percent below normal; the shortfall was 57 percent in Solapur and 49 percent in Beed. Soybean, cotton and maize have suffered heavy losses, Nashik's grape vineyards and Amravati's orange orchards are thirsting for water, and one farmer is spending three thousand rupees a day on tankers.
nazar: Drought comes from nature, but how deep it cuts is decided by the government. When compensation gets stuck in files of panchnamas (official loss assessments) and relief stops at five thousand rupees, the farmer is left with only the street. Amid Delhi's headlines, this unrest in the villages should not go unheard.
sawal: How long will the farmer bear the loss of drought alone?
ref: All India Kisan Sabha
A farmers' organisation linked to the CPI(M), which led the famous Long March from Nashik to Mumbai in 2018.
photo_note: Representative image: harvesting in a field

h: Nine parties walk out in Tamil Nadu: fix the SIR errors first
dek: The ruling TVK and the opposition DMK together left the Chief Electoral Officer's meeting and repeated the demand for the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation.
body: On 23 October, Tamil Nadu's Chief Electoral Officer Archana Patnaik called an all-party meeting at the Secretariat on the Special Summary Revision (SSR) that begins on 12 November. Nine parties, the TVK, DMK, Congress, CPI, CPI(M), VCK, NTK, AAP and DMDK, got up and left midway. The BJP, AIADMK and NPP stayed in the meeting, and the BSP did not come at all.

TVK minister CTR Nirmal Kumar said a new revision should happen only after the errors of the last SIR are fixed, and alleged that a large share of the deleted names belong to young people and women. The DMK's I. Paranthaman mentioned that about 74 lakh (7.4 million) names were cut and asked what the Commission had done to add eligible voters back. The VCK's S.S. Balaji asked how many of the 'infiltrators' in whose name the SIR was carried out were actually found, and what action was taken against them.

The AIADMK, which stayed in the meeting, also asked for a review of the deleted names. According to former minister D. Jayakumar, about 97 lakh entries were affected, of which 55 lakh were people who changed address and four lakh were duplicate names, and the Commission should make these figures clear.
nazar: When a state's government and its opposition walk out of an Election Commission meeting together, it is no small political sulk. Trust in the voter roll is the foundation of democracy, and that foundation now seems to be cracking in the south too.
sawal: 74 lakh names were cut. How many were given back?
ref: SIR and SSR
SIR is the Special Intensive Revision of the voter roll, in which every voter has to submit papers again. SSR is the ordinary Summary Revision held every year.
photo_note: Representative image: a hill village in Tamil Nadu

h: Released in deserted places at midnight: rights groups seek NHRC action
dek: Jan Hastakshep, PUCL-Delhi and Citizens for Democracy allege that anti-SIR protesters were held in police stations without water and young women were dropped at remote spots at night.
body: Three human rights groups, Jan Hastakshep, PUCL-Delhi and Citizens for Democracy, issued a joint statement on Saturday condemning the arrest and detention of those opposing the SIR. The statement is signed by Anil Dubey, T.S. Ahuja and Jyotsna Rai. They say protests at Jantar Mantar have been stopped, and wherever people gather, the police pick them up.

According to the statement, on 23 October thousands of people marched under the banner 'People Against SIR' from Gurudwara Bangla Sahib towards the Election Commission. Police and the RAF stopped them on the way, arrested students, women and trade union workers, drove them around in vehicles for a long time and locked them up in the Dwarka Sector-23 police station, where, it is alleged, they were not even given drinking water.

The groups allege that detainees were beaten, male policemen misbehaved with women, and those who asked for food, water or a toilet were abused. Young women were dropped late at night at deserted places far from Delhi's border. The groups will send a separate memorandum to the NHRC, and demand that the police take responsibility for those released, especially women, getting home safely.
nazar: If detention becomes a form of punishment, there is no need for a court at all. A girl left in a deserted place at midnight gets the message to think twice before coming onto the street next time. Only an independent inquiry into such allegations can tell whether the police stayed within the law.
sawal: Once people are released, whose job is it to see them home?
ref: PUCL
People's Union for Civil Liberties, a civil rights organisation formed in 1976 during the Emergency.

h: Farmers on Bangkok's streets: we want a right to food, not loans
dek: Outside the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, groups of Thailand's poor and its farmers demanded food sovereignty and debt cancellation, and the police blocked their way.
body: On 16 October, the international day of action for food sovereignty and against multinational corporations, Thailand's Assembly of the Poor and La Via Campesina, a worldwide alliance of farmers' movements, marched from Bangkok's Lumpini Park. Their destination was the Queen Sirikit National Convention Centre, where the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group were under way.

The protesters could not get there. When the police blocked the road, they held their ground at the Asok intersection for most of the afternoon. Crowd control units with shields were deployed on Ratchadaphisek Road, and the intersection was sealed off with iron barriers, shipping containers and detention trucks.

The groups argued that the two institutions are part of a system that weakens democracy and food sovereignty, and serves a neo-colonial structure that keeps working people down. In their view, the price of economic policies that pile debt on countries is finally paid by villages and farms.

The march put forward six demands: cancel the debt of low and middle income countries; allow a public audit of government foreign debt; end subsidies to corporations and put that money into agroecology; raise public revenue by taxing corporations and the rich; make central banks democratic and accountable; and put people and the planet, not profit, at the centre of economic policy.
The report is short and gives no crowd count or names, but it records that at the door of global finance's biggest meeting, the voice of farming was stopped with a wall of containers.
nazar: India's farmers' movement asked the same question: who will decide farm policy, the person who tills the field, or the market and the lending institutions? This picture from Bangkok is a reminder that from South Asia to Southeast Asia, small farmers fight one and the same battle: the right to their seeds, land and food, and freedom from the conditions attached to loans.
sawal: Why should loan conditions decide farm policy?
ref: Food sovereignty
The idea that how food is grown and shared should be decided by farmers and communities, not by the market or big corporations.
La Via Campesina
An international alliance of organisations of small farmers, farm workers and indigenous communities from around the world, founded in 1993.

h: Cambodia's 'Long Bay': scam hubs behind a shining tourism dream
dek: Al Jazeera's 101 East goes undercover in Cambodia to probe the empire of an alleged crime boss, where corruption and scam compounds are said to lie beneath the glitter of investment.
body: This is a film of about twenty-five minutes from 101 East, the investigative programme of Al Jazeera English, released on 10 October. The film claims that the team, working undercover in Cambodia, peeled back the layers of a business empire that, according to the allegations, is built on corruption.

At the centre of the film is the China-born billionaire Deng Pibing. According to the film's description, he has for years presented himself as a successful businessman who has contributed greatly to the development of his new homeland, Cambodia.

His most ambitious project is 'Long Bay', which is being sold as a world-class coastal destination for culture and tourism. The film takes as its subject the gap between this glossy promotion and the alleged reality behind it.

According to 101 East, the investigation reaches the scam compounds that the empire is alleged to be linked to, and also drug-fuelled karaoke parties. These are all allegations, and the film tries to test them through undercover reporting.

Background is needed to understand this film. In the past few years, online scam hubs have spread across Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos, where people lured with job offers are forced to carry out fraud. In 2023 the UN human rights office estimated that at least one lakh (100,000) people could be trapped in such hubs in Cambodia alone.

Among these victims are young people from South Asia, India included, whom the Indian government has had to rescue and bring back several times. So this probe into a big investor's alleged empire is not only Cambodia's story; it is a glimpse of the whole system in which capital, power and human trafficking get tangled together.
nazar: Many of those who end up in these scam hubs are unemployed young people from India's small towns and villages, who put their trust in an ad for a job abroad. Until there is decent work at home and strict oversight of recruitment agents, such empires built in the name of 'development' will keep getting cheap, helpless labour.
sawal: Whose labour is held hostage behind the glitter of investment?
ref: Scam compound
Closed complexes in Southeast Asia where trafficked people are forced to carry out online fraud.
101 East
Al Jazeera English's investigative documentary programme, focused on stories from the Asia-Pacific region.

h: The deep friendships of a painter of few words
dek: Sanjeev Kumar remembers the painter Ram Kumar on his birthday, in the company of Raza, Krishen Khanna and Ashok Vajpeyi.
body: Published on Jankipul on 24 October, this memoir remembers Ram Kumar, painter and Hindi fiction writer. According to the writer, this is Ram Kumar's real birthday, though some other date is recorded in many places, and every year on this day Syed Haider Raza would quietly send flowers and wine to remember him.

The story begins in Paris in 1950, when Ram Kumar went to the railway station to receive Raza and Akbar Padamsee, who had come there on French scholarships. The writer tells us that in 1985 a French government film recreated that scene, and Ram Kumar went back to take part in it.

Sanjeev Kumar got to know Ram Kumar through Ashok Vajpeyi's events and gatherings linked to Raza. He records with great affection the warmth between Raza, Ram Kumar and Krishen Khanna, and also how closely Ram Kumar followed the life of Maqbool Fida Husain. The tradition of Eid meals at Raza's home, to which Ram Kumar's wife Vimla brought heaps of sevaiyan (sweet vermicelli), is the sweetest part of this memory.

In the piece, Ram Kumar is a shy man of few words, who avoided public celebrations and whose affection showed more in his presence than in words. When Raza's health declined from late 2014, he called again and again to ask how he was, and spent one evening a month in his studio.
The writer's deepest memory is of Ram Kumar sitting silently by Raza's bed, where the friendship needed no words.
nazar: The story of modern Indian art is often told through auction prices. This memoir is a reminder that the generation was built on mutual trust, shared meals and curiosity about each other's work.
An Eid plate between Hindu and Muslim friends, sitting quietly beside a sick companion: in today's climate even these small things become a statement.
sawal: Are friendships like these still made in our art world?
ref: Ram Kumar
Hindi fiction writer and abstract painter (1924-2018), especially known for his paintings of Banaras. Nirmal Verma was his younger brother.
Syed Haider Raza
A painter known for his abstract series built around the bindu (dot), who lived in Paris for decades and returned to India in his last years.
photo_note: Young Man with Apples, Amrita Sher-Gil

h: Jholawala economics, which sees the person before the numbers
dek: Kunwar Pranjal Singh reads Jean Drèze's fifty years of work through questions of hunger, schools, jobs and caste.
body: In this long essay published on Samalochan on 24 October, Kunwar Pranjal Singh, who teaches political science at Delhi University, surveys the work of economist Jean Drèze. He says Drèze looks at economic questions not through the frame of policy but through the daily needs and rights of ordinary people, and this is what places him in the tradition of jholawala (activist, literally 'cloth-bag carrying') economics.

The essay begins with Hunger and Public Action, the book written with Amartya Sen, which drew the world's attention to hunger in India. Then comes the example of the ration system in Surguja in Chhattisgarh, where local monitoring improved grain distribution, but dealers' commission was so low that the temptation to steal remained. According to the writer, Drèze's lesson is that outcomes are decided more by the design of institutions than by money.

Pranjal Singh links Drèze to Ambedkar's idea of economic democracy. The 1996 report on basic education showed that children do not leave school because their parents are careless, but because resources and institutions do not reach them equally.

The essay treats MGNREGA as proof that organised public pressure can change policy. According to the writer, the law that replaced it in 2026 has raised the guaranteed days from 100 to 125, but questions of wages, timely payment and accountability remain open. Through Drèze's study of upper-caste dominance in Allahabad's institutions, the essay shows that he sees caste as a question of power and access.
The essay ends with Drèze's test of measuring democracy by the breadth of public debate.
nazar: That a literary magazine has published such a serious essay on an economist is itself a good thing. For the Hindi reader, Drèze's work matters because ration shops, MGNREGA and schools are exactly the places where poor, Dalit and Adivasi families meet the state.
In the era of the new employment law, it is worth remembering that a guarantee is tested not on paper but in the gram sabha (village assembly) and in timely payment.
sawal: What if the guaranteed days go up but wages still do not come on time?
ref: Jean Drèze
A Belgian-born economist who became an Indian citizen and has been part of the campaigns for the right to food and the employment guarantee.
Jholawala
A word used for activist-scholars who work on the ground, sometimes as a jibe and sometimes with respect.

h: A children's jail beyond two black gates
dek: In the first part of her memoir, Anuradha Sharma recalls the first day of a workshop at a children's jail in Faridabad.
body: This memoir, which appeared on Hindwi's Bela on 23 October, is the first part of a series. Anuradha Sharma begins by saying that life's tangles often last longer than the comfort of poems and stories. For some years she volunteered with a social reform group that talked to people begging around India Gate, and she also recalls the illness and poverty of her childhood and the moneylender who came every morning.

Around 2010-11, while she was working at a publishing and education organisation in Faridabad, her team got a government project: a few days of training for the inmates of a children's jail. One August evening she reached the building she had passed many times but had never noticed.

Two heavy black gates; inside, boys cooking and cleaning; a small child bringing tea in the jailer's office. The writer does not hide her own nervousness; she was afraid even to drink water there. The boys were seated in rows according to the kind of charge against them.

Some were interested in drawing, some in magic. One boy's drawings showed a crude way of looking at women, which troubled her. One boy hardly spoke at all. Some boys had injuries on their bodies, and the writer kept wondering whether they were beaten.
When she got back that evening, she had a severe migraine. The questions stayed with her: how did so many children end up here, and is justice being done to them?
nazar: Juvenile homes are almost missing from our public debate. This memoir makes no claim like an inquiry report, but what an outsider's eye sees, children made to work, injuries, sorting by charge, is a question in itself.
A large share of these children come from poor and marginalised families. It matters that they are written about, and we will wait for the next parts.
sawal: Who, in the end, is reformed in a reform home?
ref: Juvenile home
An institution for minors in conflict with the law. Under the juvenile justice law, its aim is not punishment but reform and rehabilitation.
Bela
Hindwi's blog section, where memoirs, diaries, reports and literary notes are published.
photo_note: A young man from the Tutinama, 16th century

h: Five memorised objections and three hours of criticism
dek: Rishabh Pratipaksh's satire takes aim at the Facebook critic who gives every new Hindi novel the same injection.
body: This satire, published on Hindwi's Bela on 23 October, opens with a warning: if you want to write a novel in Hindi, first strengthen your armour. The writer says that in the digital age, critics have multiplied many times faster than writers, and their criticism lives for only a few hours, depending on the mood of Facebook's algorithm.

No one appointed these critics. They have five ready-made objections: no originality, capitalism, thuggish publishers, cheap writers, and social media has ruined Hindi. Every new book gets the same injection.

Their ideal novel is an impossible package that must outdo Premchand, Shrilal Shukla, Nirmal Verma, Krishna Sobti and Manohar Shyam Joshi, and also take in Márquez, Dostoevsky and Camus, all in three hundred pages. The writer jokes that this is really the novel the critic wants to write himself but never does.

Break with tradition and the book is raw; follow it and it is a copy. In this way criticism becomes something that can never be proved wrong. When no flaw is found in the book, the attack on the writer's personal life begins.

The serious part is that real criticism should look at how literary forms change as society changes. According to the writer, readers who sit far from literary politics, engineers, bankers, journalists, often read with a more open mind.
nazar: Satire aside, the point hits the right nerve. In Hindi there is little real reviewing and a lot of camp politics, and the biggest losers are new writers who come from small towns without any camp behind them.
Still, dismissing criticism of capital and the publishing system as just a memorised objection is risky. The question is not to end criticism, but to write it after reading.
sawal: When did you last read a full review?
ref: Kaljayi
A work that lasts beyond its time (literally 'time-conquering'). In Hindi criticism, this word is seen as the highest level of praise.
photo_note: Horrifying News, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: Two views of Nirmal Verma, one harsh and one sympathetic
dek: On his death anniversary, Sammukh has published two essays together: Krishnamohan's sharp critique and Mukul Sharma's reading full of questions.
body: On Nirmal Verma's death anniversary on 25 October, Sammukh has placed two essays on him side by side, coming from almost opposite directions. The first is a previously published essay by the critic Krishnamohan, the second is by the young fiction writer Mukul Sharma.

Krishnamohan says Nirmal Verma's essays are an attempt to protect Indian culture from Western reason, historical sense and individualism, and that this Indianness is a selective one. He points out that traditions such as Lokayata, Buddhism, Jainism and Samkhya stood against the very ritualism that Nirmal praises. According to him, Nirmal treats Hindu and Indian as the same and comes close to the thinking of varnashrama (the caste and life-stage order). He also calls Nirmal's essay on the Kumbh romantic and self-absorbed.

Krishnamohan is even harsher on the stories. He finds the characters of Parinde (Birds), Andhere Mein (In the Dark) and Kavve aur Kala Pani (Crows and Black Water) abstract and passive, the descriptions of mist and fading light a formula, and the language weighed down by English sentence structure.

Mukul Sharma sees the same stories as a world of questions, like a child making the familiar world strange. For him, the question of sin in Aadmi aur Ladki (The Man and the Girl) is a question of who has the right to pass judgment on private experience. He answers progressive critics by saying that the hunger of one night in London and the unemployment of one September evening show that Nirmal was not unaware of material conditions.
Read together, the two essays make Nirmal Verma seem not a closed case but an open debate.
nazar: Now that cultural nationalism has become the language of power, this debate on Nirmal Verma's Indianness is no longer only literary. That is why Krishnamohan's critique feels sharp, even if at places it reads like a verdict.
Mukul Sharma's defence is a reminder that a fiction writer's essays and his stories are not the same thing. The good thing is that Sammukh has given both voices room on the same page.
sawal: Can a writer's stories be bigger than his ideas?
ref: Nirmal Verma
A leading writer of the Nayi Kahani (New Story) movement (1929-2005), whose stories keep returning to the hills of Shimla and the cold evenings of Europe.
Lokayata
A materialist school of philosophy in ancient India, also called Charvaka philosophy.

h: A grain stuck to the millstone's peg, and days of illness
dek: Nitesh Vyas's prose is the daybook of a restless mind, moving between death, Kabir, loneliness and news from Jantar Mantar.
body: Published on Sammukh on 24 October, this prose piece by Nitesh Vyas is split into many short fragments, like pages of a diary. The first fragment is about death. For the writer, death is not an event but a slow process, and life a chain of small stations where the train stops for air and water. An old illness walks with him through his days, and he wonders what will happen to his wife and child after him.

The second fragment is about Kabir, whom he calls the poet of the common man, who reaches everywhere, from folk singers and qawwals to expensive hotels. Listening to a Kabir bhajan in Fareed Ayaz's voice, he reflects on the image of the chakki (grinding mill), whose two stones of profit and loss, praise and blame, joy and sorrow grind down everything caught between them.

The cure too lies with the same saints. He recalls the saying of Kamal, Kabir's son, that the grain which stays stuck to the peg in the middle escapes being ground. The writer remembers the hand mill of his childhood home, now gone, and the ideal of living in the world without being eaten by it.

The other fragments are about restlessness, a handful of friends and solitude, into which noise keeps breaking in. Drawing on Agyeya and Gagan Ji, he reflects on sorrow: that sorrow cannot be handed over to anyone else.

The last fragment is an evening after rain, with children playing cricket on the roof talking about the news from Jantar Mantar. The writer thinks that where there should have been conversation, there are now lathis (batons), tear gas and stones.
nazar: This prose begins with private grief and ends with public grief, and that is its strength. That protests and lathi charges are on children's lips shows that politics has now reached the rooftop of the home.
Kabir's image of the millstones is as apt as ever for the common person caught in the middle.
sawal: Who is being ground between the two stones today?
ref: Kamal
A saint poet traditionally believed to be Kabir's son, to whom many sayings and couplets in folk tradition are linked.
Nishkam karma
The idea from the Gita that one should act but not be attached to the fruits of action.
